settings.title: Flat-Fee Nil T2 Filing for Roofing Corporations

settings.editor:
Roofing stops and starts with the weather, and a corporation can go a full year without a roof on it. What tends to happen in that year is small and easy to forget: a load of torn-off metal weighed in, a warranty callback that bills nobody, a few bundles sold to another crew. A year with none of it is $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Whether the crew was paid off, the season was given to a competitor, the truck was sold, or the work went into a newer corporation, the year is measured against roofs installed or repaired and invoiced, scrap or material sold on, any warranty allowance received and whether a vehicle or a hoist left. Schedules 100, 125, 141 and 50 are prepared and the return is transmitted electronically. A year with revenue in it goes to the full service.

settings.title_text: A Season Missed Is Not a Year Skipped
settings.description_text: No roofs changes the figures the return reports. Dissolution is the only thing that stops there being a return.

settings.title_text: Warranty Work Earns Nothing and Still Happens
settings.description_text: A workmanship promise can pull a crew back onto a finished roof years later. The day costs money and raises no invoice.

settings.title_text: Suppliers and Insurers Read the Record
settings.description_text: A supply account reopened, or roofing liability cover renewed, is read by somebody who looks at the filings.

settings.title_text: The Truck and the Hoist Are Property
settings.description_text: A truck, a hoist and a compressor belong to the corporation until they are sold or taken out of it.

settings.editor:
What keeps these corporations alive is usually the plan to go again in the spring, or a workmanship warranty with years left to run on it. Both are good reasons to hold the company, and neither of them is a reason the return stops being due.

A year with no roof and no scrap sale is $300.00 plus HST per tax year. Outstanding years go in date order so the stock and truck figures agree.

settings.html:
The year is nil

  • No roof was installed, repaired or invoiced by the corporation
  • No scrap metal or leftover material was sold by it
  • No warranty allowance or supplier credit was received
  • No truck, hoist or compressor left by sale
  • Nothing in its name paid interest

The year is not nil

  • Scrap metal or torn-off material was weighed in and paid for
  • A roof went on, or a repair was billed to somebody
  • Shingles or rolls went to another crew for money
  • A manufacturer credit or warranty allowance arrived
  • The truck, the hoist or a gun changed hands

Due either way

  • No season off excuses a year end
  • Each return waits on a signed T183CORP
  • Schedule 50 lists holdings at a tenth or more
  • The liability policy and any trade registration renew separately
  • A clearance certificate comes before dissolution

settings.title: Roofing Corporation Filing Across Canada

settings.editor:
Roofing corporations are filed the same way wherever the registered office sits, because the return is prepared and transmitted electronically from end to end. There is nothing to print, nothing to post and nothing to sign in person.

Where the corporation was incorporated changes the registry, not the return. An Ontario corporation answers to the Ontario Business Registry, and corporations in British Columbia, Alberta, Quebec and Saskatchewan each answer to their own. The T2 itself is federal and identical in all of them. Within Ontario, a corporation registered in Toronto, Mississauga, Brampton or Ottawa is filed on the same terms and at the same price as one anywhere else in the country.

Two provinces add a return the federal T2 does not cover. A Quebec corporation also files the CO-17 and an Alberta corporation also files the AT1. Both are separate provincial returns, and neither is included in the $300.00 plus HST fee.
